explanations.answer: To be cursed and cut off from Christ
explanations.explanation: Yes, baker. Paul, the apostle writing this letter, says, “…I could wish that I myself were cursed and cut off from Christ for the sake of my brothers…” That's how much his heart hurts for them. I've never cared about anybody enough to wish that, and I once gave up the last cookie in the box for a neighbor and cried about it.

explanations.answer: To be locked in prison for life
explanations.explanation: Good guess, friend, since Paul is serious here. But verse 3 never mentions prison. Paul says he could wish himself “cursed and cut off from Christ,” and that's a much deeper kind of hurt. Whatever he's feeling, the text says it's for the sake of his brothers, his own flesh and blood.

explanations.answer: To lose his calling as an apostle
explanations.explanation: That one sounds sensible, baker, but it's not on the page. Paul says he could wish that he himself were “cursed and cut off from Christ.” The wish is about being cut off from Christ, not about his job. And he says it for the sake of his brothers, his own flesh and blood.
That's it, friend. Paul calls them “the people of Israel” in verse 4, and he says they're his own flesh and blood. He's writing about his own family here. I think that's why his sorrow runs so deep.

Close to the letter, baker, since Rome is where Paul is sending it. But the believers in Rome are the ones receiving his words. The people he's grieving over are named in verse 4 as the people of Israel.
Nice try, friend, but Greece never shows up in these verses. Paul names his own flesh and blood plainly: “the people of Israel.” Then he starts listing what belongs to them. It's a long list.

Right, baker. Paul says “from them proceeds the human descent of Christ, who is God over all, forever worthy of praise! Amen.” He doesn't just stop at the family tree. He ends it with praise, and that tells you how he feels about Christ.

Not quite, friend. Verse 5 says the human descent of Christ proceeds from Israel's people. Then Paul adds that Christ “is God over all, forever worthy of praise! Amen.” Both parts are right there in the same verse.

explanations.answer: Not all descended from Israel are Israel
explanations.explanation: That's the one, baker. Paul says, “…not all who are descended from Israel are Israel.” God's word hasn't fallen apart. Paul is saying the people it speaks of aren't simply everyone born into the family line.

explanations.answer: All of Israel kept the law perfectly
explanations.explanation: I can see why you'd reach for that, friend, but Paul never says it. His reason in verse 6 is this: “…not all who are descended from Israel are Israel.” Nothing in these verses says everyone kept the law perfectly. His whole point is about who counts as Israel.

explanations.answer: The promises were never for Israel
explanations.explanation: Careful, baker, because Paul says the opposite in verse 4. He lists the promises right there among the things that belong to the people of Israel. His reason in verse 6 is that “…not all who are descended from Israel are Israel.”
Yes, friend. Paul quotes, “Through Isaac your offspring will be reckoned.” Isaac was Abraham's son. Paul is showing that the promise runs through one particular son, not just any son.

Good thinking, baker, because Ishmael was Abraham's son too (Genesis 16:15). But the Scripture Paul quotes names someone else: “Through Isaac your offspring will be reckoned.” So being a son of Abraham wasn't the whole story.
Joseph is a famous name, friend. He was Jacob's son (Genesis 30:24). But the Scripture Paul quotes is about Abraham's offspring, and it says, “Through Isaac your offspring will be reckoned.”

I get why you'd say it, baker, but the verse goes the other way. Paul says, “So it is not the children of the flesh who are God's children…” Instead, “…it is the children of the promise who are regarded as offspring.” So the promise decides it, not the family line.

That's right, friend. Paul says it is not the children of the flesh who are God's children. It's the children of the promise who are regarded as offspring. You can't just be born into this one. It runs on the promise.
That's right, baker. The promise says, “At the appointed time I will return, and Sarah will have a son.” Sarah was Abraham's wife. The promise came first, and then came Isaac.
Hagar is in Abraham's story, friend. She was Sarai's servant (Genesis 16:1). But the promise Paul quotes names someone else: “…Sarah will have a son.”
Leah is from a later chapter of the family story, baker. She married Jacob (Genesis 29:23, 25). The promise Paul quotes in verse 9 says, “…Sarah will have a son.”

I see why you might think so, baker, but Paul says the opposite. It was “before the twins were born or had done anything good or bad” that Rebecca was told. They hadn't done a thing yet. The word came first.
Right, friend. Paul says it was “before the twins were born or had done anything good or bad.” Nobody had earned anything yet. Paul says it's “not by works but by Him who calls.”

explanations.answer: The older will serve the younger
explanations.explanation: You've got it, baker. Rebecca was told, “The older will serve the younger.” That's backwards from how families usually work. Paul says it came “not by works but by Him who calls.”

explanations.answer: The younger will serve the older
explanations.explanation: That's how it usually goes, friend, so I get the guess. But Rebecca was told, “The older will serve the younger.” Paul says that came “not by works but by Him who calls.” The usual order got flipped.

explanations.answer: The two will share the land
explanations.explanation: That would be a tidy ending, baker, but verse 12 doesn't say it. Rebecca was told, “The older will serve the younger.” That's the word Paul quotes.
Yes, baker. The line says, “Jacob I loved, but Esau I hated.” It's a heavy line, and Paul quotes it plainly. Paul is quoting what was written.

I understand the mix-up, friend, since the line names both twins. But it says, “Jacob I loved, but Esau I hated.” The love goes with Jacob. I think this is a hard line to read, and it's okay to say so.

I get the instinct, baker, since this line is hard to read. But Paul quotes, “Jacob I loved, but Esau I hated.” The line names Jacob as the one loved. It's heavy, and I think we should read it slowly.
That's it, friend. Paul asks, “Is God unjust?” and answers right away, “Certainly not!” He doesn't hedge or add an exception. The next verses are where he explains.
I see why you'd think that, baker, since Esau was just named. But Paul gives no exception. He says, “Certainly not!” and that covers the whole question.
Honest guess, friend, and people do wonder about it. But Paul doesn't say it seems so. He says, “Certainly not!” Then he goes straight to what God said to Moses.

explanations.answer: He'll have mercy on whom I have mercy
explanations.explanation: Yes, baker. Paul says God told Moses, “I will have mercy on whom I have mercy, and I will have compassion on whom I have compassion.” Mercy belongs to God to give. Nobody can order it up like a tray of cookies.

explanations.answer: He'll have mercy on all who keep the law
explanations.explanation: Reasonable guess, friend, but that's not what God told Moses. Paul quotes, “I will have mercy on whom I have mercy, and I will have compassion on whom I have compassion.” Paul then says it “does not depend on man's desire or effort, but on God's mercy.”

explanations.answer: He'll have mercy on Israel's priests only
explanations.explanation: That's a narrow one, baker, and the text doesn't say it. Paul quotes God saying to Moses, “I will have mercy on whom I have mercy…” No group is named in that line.
Exactly, friend. Paul says, “So then, it does not depend on man's desire or effort, but on God's mercy.” You can't bake your way into it with extra effort. It's a gift.
I see the pull of that one, baker, since the law was just listed among Israel's gifts. But verse 16 says it depends “on God's mercy.” The law isn't what Paul points to there.
The temple worship did show up in the list in verse 4, friend. But in verse 16 Paul says it “does not depend on man's desire or effort, but on God's mercy.” Mercy is the word.
That's it, baker. The Scripture says, “I raised you up for this very purpose, that I might display My power in you…” Pharaoh was the king of Egypt in Moses' day. God's power was on display in him.

Mercy is a big word in this passage, friend, so I see why you'd pick it. But the Scripture said to Pharaoh, “I raised you up for this very purpose, that I might display My power in you…” The word there is power.
Wisdom is a fine word, baker, but it's not the one here. The Scripture says to Pharaoh, “…that I might display My power in you…” Power is what God says He'll show.
Not quite, baker. The Scripture says God raised Pharaoh up so “…that My name might be proclaimed in all the earth.” It's not only Egypt. It's all the earth.
Right, friend. The Scripture says, “…that My name might be proclaimed in all the earth.” All the earth is much bigger than Egypt. And it's the same verse that talks about power.
Yes, baker. Paul says someone will ask, “Then why does God still find fault? For who can resist His will?” He puts the pushback right on the table. Then he answers it.

explanations.answer: Why God chose Israel at all
explanations.explanation: Good thinking, friend, since Israel's all over this chapter. But the question Paul expects in verse 19 is, “Then why does God still find fault?” That's the one he answers next.
That's an honest question, baker, but Paul doesn't raise it here. The question he expects is, “Then why does God still find fault? For who can resist His will?”

Right, baker. Paul asks, “Shall what is formed say to Him who formed it, ‘Why did You make me like this?’” It's a picture of the made talking back to the maker. He sets that picture next to the question people raised.

That one's actually in the text, friend. Paul says, “Shall what is formed say to Him who formed it, ‘Why did You make me like this?’” It's a picture of the formed talking back to the One who formed it.

explanations.answer: A special vessel and a common one
explanations.explanation: Yes, friend. Paul says the potter can make “…one vessel for special occasions and another for common use.” Both come from the same lump of clay. It's a picture of the potter's right.
That would make for a very plain shelf, baker. But Paul says the potter can make “one vessel for special occasions and another for common use” from the same clay. So there are two kinds.
That would be a strange workshop, friend. Paul says the potter has “the right to make” from the same lump. It's the potter's right, not the clay's.
That's it, baker. Paul says God “bore with great patience the vessels of His wrath, prepared for destruction.” Patience is the word he picks. It's right there in verse 22.
I see why wrath makes you think of that, friend. But Paul says God “bore with great patience” the vessels of His wrath. The text says patience, not quick anger.
Reasonable guess, baker, but verse 22 doesn't say that. It says God “bore with great patience the vessels of His wrath, prepared for destruction.” Patience is what Paul names.
Exactly, friend. Paul says, “…whom He has called not only from the Jews, but also from the Gentiles.” Gentiles are people who aren't Jewish. So the calling reaches both.
I see the logic, baker, since warning was nearby in the chapter. But verse 24 says “…whom He has called not only from the Jews, but also from the Gentiles.” Called is the word.
Good try, friend, but tested isn't there. Verse 24 says God has “called” them, “not only from the Jews, but also from the Gentiles.”
Yes, baker. God says in Hosea, “I will call them ‘My People’ who are not My people…” Hosea was a prophet in Israel. People once called not His own get a new name from Him.
Servants is a natural guess, friend, but it's not the name. Hosea's line says, “I will call them ‘My People’ who are not My people…” The new name is My People.
That's a friendly one, baker, but the text doesn't say it. The line from Hosea is, “I will call them ‘My People’ who are not My people…” That's the name God gives.

Yes, friend. Paul quotes, “It will happen that in the very place where it was said to them, ‘You are not My people,’ they will be called ‘sons of the living God.’” The same place where they heard no gets a new answer.
This one is actually in the text, baker. Paul quotes, “It will happen that in the very place where it was said to them, ‘You are not My people,’ they will be called ‘sons of the living God.’”
That's it, baker. Isaiah says, “Though the number of the Israelites is like the sand of the sea, only the remnant will be saved.” The number is huge, but the remnant is who's named.
The sand of the sea does sound like plenty, friend. But Isaiah says, “…only the remnant will be saved.” It's a big crowd, and the remnant is the part named.
Nice guess, baker, but priests aren't mentioned here. Isaiah says, “Though the number of the Israelites is like the sand of the sea, only the remnant will be saved.”
Not quite, baker. Isaiah says the Lord “will carry out His sentence on the earth thoroughly and decisively.” That's the opposite of slow and halfway.
Right, friend. Isaiah says, “For the Lord will carry out His sentence on the earth thoroughly and decisively.” Thoroughly and decisively, not halfway.
Yes, baker. Isaiah says, “Unless the Lord of Hosts had left us descendants, we would have become like Sodom, we would have resembled Gomorrah.” The descendants left to them make the difference.
Those are big cities, friend, and they're in the Bible. But Isaiah's line names other cities: “…we would have become like Sodom, we would have resembled Gomorrah.”
Good try, baker, since those cities are in the Bible too. But Isaiah says, “…we would have become like Sodom, we would have resembled Gomorrah.” Those are the two.
